replacement: 13. But let us turn back. The self-contradiction that seems to show itself among the ascetics, "Life turned against Life," is simply nonsense — this much is absolutely obvious — when judged from the physiological standpoint and not, now, the psychological one. It can only be an apparent contradiction. It has to be a kind of provisional expression, an explanation, a formula, an adjustment: a psychological misunderstanding of something whose real nature could not be grasped for a long time, and whose real essence could not be described. It is a mere word jammed into an old gap in human knowledge. Put briefly, the facts that count against its being real are these. The ascetic ideal comes out of the protective, self-preserving instincts of a decadent life, a life that tries by every means it has to hold its position and fight for its existence. It points to a partial physiological depression and exhaustion, and the deepest, still intact life-instincts keep fighting this ceaselessly with new weapons and new discoveries. The ascetic ideal is one such weapon. So its position is exactly the reverse of what its worshippers imagine: life is struggling in it and through it with death and against death, and the ascetic ideal is a dodge to keep life going. History teaches something important about how far this ideal could rule over man and exercise power over him, especially in every place where the civilization and taming of man was completed. What it shows is the diseased state of man up to now, at any rate of the tamed man: his physiological struggle with death (more precisely, with disgust with life, with exhaustion, with the wish for the "end"). The ascetic priest is the incarnate wish for an existence of another kind, on another plane. He is, in fact, the highest point of this wish, its official ecstasy and passion. Yet the very strength of this wish is the fetter that ties him down here. It is just this that turns him into a tool, one who has to labor to create more favorable conditions for earthly existence, for existence on the human plane. With this very strength he holds the whole herd of failures, distortions, abortions, unfortunates and sufferers from themselves of every kind fast to existence, while he walks instinctively ahead of them as their herdsman. You understand me already: this ascetic priest, this apparent enemy of life, this denier — he actually belongs among the really great conservative and affirmative forces of life.... Where does this diseased state come from? For man is more diseased, more uncertain, more changeable and more unstable than any other animal, there is no doubt of it — he is the diseased animal. So where does it spring from? Certainly he has also dared more, innovated more, braved more and challenged fate more than all the other animals put together. He is the great experimenter with himself, the unsatisfied, the insatiate, who fights for supreme mastery against beast, Nature and gods. He is the as yet ever uncompelled, the ever future, who can no longer find any rest from his own aggressive strength, driven mercilessly on by the spur of the future dug into the flesh of the present. How could so brave and rich an animal fail to be also the most endangered, the animal with the longest and deepest sickness among all sick animals?... Man grows sick of it, and often enough whole epidemics of this satiety break out (as around 1348, the time of the Dance of Death). Yet even this very nausea, this tiredness, this disgust with himself, is thrown off by him with such force that it is at once made into a new fetter. His "nay" to life brings forth, as though by magic, an abundance of graceful "yeas"; and even when he wounds himself, this master of destruction and of self-destruction, it is the wound itself afterward that forces him to live.

replacement: 17. But is he really a physician, this ascetic priest? We already understand why we are scarcely allowed to call him one, however much he likes to feel like a "saviour" and to be worshipped as one. He combats only the actual suffering, the sufferer's discomfort, not its cause, not the actual state of sickness. This must be our most radical objection to priestly medication. Yet put yourself just once into that point of view, which the priests have a monopoly on, and you will find it hard to exhaust your amazement at all he has seen, sought and found from that standpoint. The mitigation of suffering, every kind of "consoling" — all this shows itself as his very genius. With what ingenuity has he interpreted his mission as consoler, with what aplomb and audacity has he chosen the weapons the part requires! Christianity in particular should be called a great treasure-chamber of ingenious consolations, so great a store of refreshing, soothing, deadening drugs has it piled up within itself. It has hazarded so many of the most dangerous and daring expedients; with such subtlety and refinement, Oriental refinement, it has divined which emotional stimulants can conquer, at least for a time, the deep depression, the leaden fatigue and the black melancholy of physiological cripples. For, speaking generally, all religions are mainly concerned with fighting a certain fatigue and heaviness that has infected everything. You can take it as prima facie probable that in certain places in the world there was almost bound to prevail from time to time, among large masses of the population, a sense of physiological depression. Owing to their lack of physiological knowledge, this did not appear to their consciousness as such, and so its "cause" and its cure could only be sought and tried in the science of moral psychology (this, in fact, is my most general formula for what is generally called a "religion"). Such a feeling of depression can have the most diverse origins. It may result from the crossing of too heterogeneous races (or of classes — genealogical and racial differences also show themselves in the classes: the European "Weltschmerz," the "Pessimism" of the nineteenth century, is really the result of an absurd and sudden class-mixture). It may be brought about by a mistaken emigration, a race falling into a climate for which its power of adaptation is insufficient (the case of the Indians in India). It may be the effect of old age and fatigue (the Parisian pessimism from 1850 onwards). It may come from a wrong diet (the alcoholism of the Middle Ages, the nonsense of vegetarianism — though these have in their favor the authority of Sir Christopher in Shakespeare). It may come from blood-deterioration, malaria, syphilis and the like (German depression after the Thirty Years' War, which infected half of Germany with evil diseases and thereby paved the way for German servility, for German pusillanimity). In such a case a war on a grand scale against the feeling of depression is invariably attempted. Let us inform ourselves briefly about its most important practices and phases (I leave aside, as stands to reason, the actual philosophic war against the feeling of depression, which is usually simultaneous — it is interesting enough, but too absurd, too practically negligible, too full of cobwebs, too much of a hole-and-corner affair, especially when pain is proved to be a mistake, on the naïf hypothesis that pain must needs vanish once the mistake underlying it is recognized — but behold! it does anything but vanish ...). That dominant depression is fought primarily by weapons that reduce the consciousness of life itself to the lowest degree. Wherever possible, no more wishes, no more wants; avoid everything that produces emotion, that produces "blood" (eating no salt, the fakir hygiene); no love; no hate; equanimity; no revenge; no getting rich; no work; begging; as far as possible, no woman, or as little woman as possible; as far as the intellect is concerned, Pascal's principle, "il faut s'abêtir." In ethical and psychological language, the result is "self-annihilation," "sanctification"; in physiological language, "hypnotism." It is the attempt to find some approximate human equivalent for what hibernation is for certain animals and æstivation for many tropical plants: a minimum of assimilation and metabolism in which life just manages to subsist without really entering the consciousness. An amazing amount of human energy has been devoted to this object — perhaps uselessly? There cannot be the slightest doubt that these sportsmen of "saintliness," of whom nearly every nation has at times had an abundance, really found a genuine relief from what they fought with such rigorous training. In countless cases they really did escape deep physiological depression with the help of their system of hypnotism, and their method is consequently counted among the most universal ethnological facts. Similarly it is improper to treat such a plan of starving the physical element and the desires as itself a symptom of insanity (as a clumsy species of roast-beef-eating "freethinkers" and Sir Christophers are fain to do). All the more certain is it that their method can and does pave the way to all kinds of mental disturbances, for instance "inner lights" (as with the Hesychasts of Mount Athos), auditory and visual hallucinations, voluptuous ecstasies and effervescences of sensualism (the history of St. Theresa). The explanation the victims give of such events is always the acme of fanatical falsehood; this is self-evident. Note well, however, the tone of implicit gratitude that rings in the very will to an explanation of such a character. They always regard the supreme state, salvation itself, that final goal of universal hypnosis and peace, as the mystery of mysteries, which even the most supreme symbols are inadequate to express. They regard it as an entry and homecoming to the essence of things, a liberation from all illusions, "knowledge," "truth," "being," an escape from every end, every wish, every action, something even beyond Good and Evil.
